query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex, initially single‐phase high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior under demanding service conditions emerges not from traditional grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation but from a transient, deformation-induced nanophase (such as local amorphization or nanocavitation) that forms preferentially along high-angle grain boundaries under high strain rate and cyclic thermal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenous, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with stabilized solid solution microstructure and minimal grain-boundary segregation or preexisting precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to controlled high strain rate mechanical testing combined with cyclic thermal loading in an inert or ultra-high vacuum environment.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant regimes that include both high-temperature (to probe softening tendencies) and low-temperature (to explore embrittlement) with cyclic loading; performed in environments that exclude oxidation or impurity-driven effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Transient formation of a localized nanophase (amorphous regions or cavitated grain-boundary layers) at high-angle grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under extreme mechanical and thermal fluctuations, localized plastic deformation at grain boundaries triggers transient nanostructural transformations (such as dynamic amorphization or cavitation). These changes reduce intergranular cohesion, promoting brittle grain-boundary decohesion even in the absence of chemical segregation or stable secondary precipitates found in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline conditions, samples experiencing high strain rate and cyclical thermal loading will show a marked reduction in toughness accompanied by signs of brittle fracture, with observable transient nanostructural changes at the grain boundaries during in-situ characterization.
generation.baseline: The initial ductile, tough behavior of the HEA observed under moderate strain rate and isothermal conditions, where the microstructure remains homogenous and free of nanophase alterations.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be significant only under high strain rate and cyclic thermal conditions; under static or low rate, isothermal conditions, the HEA should retain its ductile characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature (amorphous versus nanocavitated) and the critical thresholds (in terms of strain rate and temperature cycling amplitude) for the formation of the transient nanophase are not yet fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. Subject one set to high strain rate cyclic thermal loading (mimicking harsh service conditions) and the other set to moderate, isothermal loading. Use in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and diffraction methods to monitor grain-boundary structural changes and nanophase formation during deformation. Concurrently, measure mechanical properties including fracture toughness and stress–strain responses.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_Ic) and ductility from stress–strain curves
Grain-boundary structure via in-situ TEM imaging and selected area electron diffraction
Onset and evolution of any transient nanophase formation (amorphous or cavitated regions)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under high strain rate cyclic thermal loading (compared with isothermal controls) there is no observable formation of a transient nanophase at grain boundaries and no corresponding reduction in toughness (i.e., the HEA behaves similarly to the control), then the hypothesis that brittleness emerges via transient nanophase-induced grain-boundary decohesion is falsified.

Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. frame.system: An initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy that is engineered for demanding engineering service with inherent resistance to conventional grain-boundary segregation, intermetallic precipitation, and rapid grain coarsening.
frame.goal: To establish a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges in these alloys, distinguishing its mechanism from that of conventional alloys.
frame.limitation: Existing observations in high-entropy alloys do not clearly identify the mechanism behind toughness degradation, as the usual culprits in conventional alloys (e.g., grain-boundary segregation and precipitates) are largely suppressed.
constraints: avoid modifications that compromise the inherent benefits (e.g., suppression of grain growth and intermetallic formation)
frame.regime: Comparative mechanical testing under service-relevant conditions, including a range of temperatures (both high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement regimes) and loading rates, to isolate the effects of any potential novel deformation or phase transformation mechanism.
prior_attempts: In conventional alloys, toughness degradation was linked to grain-boundary segregation and precipitation, but such phenomena are suppressed in high-entropy alloys, leaving a gap in understanding.
Prior evidence on microstructural stability in high-entropy alloys shows resistance to common degradation paths, prompting the need for a new explanatory mechanism.
